https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, McLaren's Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix last season By Andrew Benson F1 Correspondent at the Hungaroring Published 25 July 2026 McLaren's Lando Norris took his first grand prix pole position of the season in Hungary - but Lewis Hamilton was denied the chance to make it an all-British front row by a penalty for impeding. A three-place penalty for blocking Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri has dropped Hamilton to fifth on the grid, and may have erased his chances of a ninth victory on a track he has almost made his own in his 20-year career. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who originally qualified fourth, was also given a three-place grid penalty for not slowing sufficiently under single yellow flags, following a spin for Red Bull's Max Verstappen at the final corner. The penalties mean Ferrari's Charles Leclerc will start second, Piastri third, Verstappen fourth and Hamilton fifth, with Mercedes' George Russell sixth, a place ahead of team-mate Antonelli. Hamilton had been fastest on the first runs, by just over 0.1secs from Norris, but neither the seven-time champion nor Leclerc could improve on their final attempts. Verstappen's error affected Antonelli and Russell, who were forced to slow, although in the Italian's case the stewards decided it was not by enough. Verstappen had got going again before Norris came around as the last driver on track to clinch pole in the upgraded McLaren by just 0.012 seconds. Norris cautious despite pole as it 'falls apart' for Hamilton Published 25 July Malaysia set to host F1 race in October Published 26 July Norris said: "Very happy to be back on top, especially at a track where you certainly want to be on pole. "I had confidence the whole of today. My laps in Q3 were not the best, even the one at the end, so pleasantly surprised to be on top." Hamilton was a second slower on his second run than on his first and was unhappy he had been sent out for it first. "I had a clean out-lap, and when I started my lap, already into Turn One I had a snap and I was already 0.15secs down," Hamilton said. "It just cascaded from there. "So, the last lap was the worst lap of all, and all the other laps were really good. We clearly had the car to be on pole today, and I just didn't deliver. So that's tough to swallow." On the impeding scenario, Hamilton said he had not been warned of Piastri's approach by the team: "I was told literally when he was at the apex behind me, so I had no idea he was coming. "I was the first out, so I thought everyone had finished their lap. Charles, I think, was the car that was behind me when I left the pit lane, as far as I was aware. So, yeah, crazy, because it had been clean, and obviously it wasn't intentional." Verstappen railed about the unpredictable handling of the Red Bull over the radio after his spin. His team-mate Isack Hadjar starts eighth, ahead of Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg. Alonso 'optimistic' after progressing to Q2 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Aston Martin team members celebrate Fernando Alonso's progress into Q2 Fernando Alonso made a major breakthrough for Aston Martin on the weekend they debuted their virtually new car by breaking out of the first session for the first time this season. Alonso will start 16th, 2.8secs off pole - but that was two seconds faster in relative pace than they had managed for some time. The veteran Spaniard, who is 45 next week, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I feel relieved a little bit, feeling that the team understood the weaknesses of the car and this is the first step in the right direction. "We brought a few updates to this car early in the season, and it didn't work much. And we come from two years of disappointments of upgrades. So definitely there is a change in optimism in the factory and I feel optimistic." Alonso faces a decision this summer as to whether to continue his career after this season. He said that while he had no doubts managing technical partner Adrian Newey would lead the team to success in the future, he was not sure whether it would happen soon enough for him. "No-one should doubt Adrian Newey or the potential we have in Silverstone. It is a matter of time before we have the best chassis and it is a matter of time before Honda have the best engine in F1. It is a question of when." All the drivers were battling with a Hungaroring track surface that was breaking up, especially in the final two corners, where Norris said it was especially difficult to judge the grip level. Even before the incident with Verstappen, Russell was afflicted on his final run by a water leak, which was spraying water on to his rear tyres. Mercedes asked him to pull over immediately after crossing the line, and he parked at Turn One, in an attempt to avoid damaging the engine. Speaking before his penalty, Antonelli said: "I think we were just slightly out of the window with tyres, then in Q3 we did a good step and the car just felt finally a bit more alive. For sure it was a shame with the yellow flags, but it happens. P3 was on the table today but still not good enough for pole." https://news.postimees.ee/7412824/girls-.text: Customer Care Subscriptions Announcements Advertising Cookie Settings Privacy Policy RUS EST ESTONIAN NEWS Girls of the «Estonian school» defying poverty and fear of explosion Jaanus Piirsalu ajakirjanik Erik Prozes pressifotograaf 20th December 2021, 14:49 Fatima Zahra school. Photo: Erik Prozes Taliban fighters came by once and asked what the school was teaching, took a brief look around and left without saying another word, Jamila Hakimi (26), head of a girls’ school in Jalalabad, said. The school has continued teaching as before. It happened in September, soon after Afghanistan had fallen to the Taliban. The group intervened in the life of the school again and in a much more abrupt way last Sunday. The school that has been operating for a decade with support from Estonian NGO Mondo is located in a Jalalabad suburb, near an olive oil factory. The schoolhouse stands in the middle of a field lined with clay residences. The children who go to the school live on the edge of the field, a few hundred meters from the schoolhouse. The Taliban attacked one of the houses at 3 a.m. last Sunday, claiming it was inhabited by Islamic State fighters. The Taliban claimed that ten IS fighters were killed in the offensive but did not reveal its own casualties as the organization never does. Jamila Hakimi (26), head of a girls’ school in Jalalabad. Photo: Erik Prozes “Half the children did not show up at school the next day,” Jamila Hakimi said. Luckily, all the students returned the day after. The school that was fixed up and is still funded by Estonian private sponsors and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs is currently teaching 285 girls in grades one through six. Most of them are Pashtuns between the ages of 7 and 13. The school is named after the daughter of Prophet Muhammad Fatima Zahra. High schools still closed The school week runs from Sunday to Thursday as Friday is the holy day of Muslims. School starts at 7.30 in the morning and ends at 11.30 a.m. – there are five classes every day. The day always starts with religion class or studying the Quran. The girls also learn Dari, Pashto and English, mathematics, science and geography. The Taliban has only allowed elementary schools of grades one through six to be opened for girls. Most local high schools (grades 7-12) are closed, even though the Taliban has promised girls’ high schools will be opened as the “situation stabilizes.” Bilal Karimi, deputy for spokesman for the Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan and the Taliban Zabiullah Mujahid, said in an interview to Postimees that girls’ high schools will be opened in all provinces by spring at the latest. They are currently open in around ten of Afghanistan’s 34 provinces. The BBC confirmed this week that schools for older girls have indeed been opened in some western and northern provinces. It is also said that girls’ high schools are open in Jalalabad. “The Taliban is doing nothing for the children’s education, but at least they are not bothering us, which is the most important thing right now,” English teacher at the “Estonian school” Hajeera Sadaqat (23) said. Fatima Zahra said that even though the Taliban did not close elementary schools, 15 families pulled their girls out of school after the Taliban came to power. Specifically, they did not send their kids back to school on September 1. “They said that their daughters do not need an education,” Hakimi said. Poverty and late dads Poverty that has followed in the wake of the Taliban is also affecting girls’ school attendance. Most girls have lost their fathers in the conflict between the previous authority and the Taliban. Families are supported by mothers who have no work (without exception) or relatives. The teachers see extreme poverty on a daily basis. Poverty that has followed in the wake of the Taliban is also affecting girls’ school attendance. Photo: Erik Prozes “Parents have come in the middle of lessons and pulled their kids out class to so they could go and collect firewood,” Hakimi said. “Some children work before the school day starts (at 7.30 a.m.!), for example, cleaning shops for which they are paid 10-15 afghanis.” That comes to 8-12 euro cents. The young principal Hakimi told us about crushing child poverty with a passionless voice. It is merely a fact that she has become accustomed to. “We can see that a lot of the children are undernourished. We have more than 15 children in whose case I know that they have almost nothing to eat at home. They are very hungry when they come to school,” she said. The school does not offer meals. There is no money for it. There is no money for anything. The teachers haven’t been paid in four months or since the schoolyear began. Their salaries were paid by NGO Mondo until recently, while UN sanctions have made transfers impossible. The school could not buy new textbooks and workbooks this fall as funding for that had also come from the Estonian nonprofit. Teachers asked families to buy text- and workbooks, while they knew the answer. We do not even have money to buy food, and you are talking about books. “Some families are trying. A lot of students collect firewood for sale and use the money to buy textbooks,” Hakimi said. The principal proceeded to give other examples of poverty but ended on a very important note: “We, the teachers, try our best without pay. I think that students should not hide behind poverty. It is no reason [not to learn].” 50-70 students per class Teacher Hajeera Sadaqat said that a class has 50-70 students. Classrooms are full of children sitting packed next to one another on the floor, with textbooks and notebooks on the ground in front of them. Everyone is intently listening to the teacher. “They are very well-behaved and always listen to me,” Sadaqat told us. “We could not teach them if they weren’t.” All the girls are extremely shy and careful about answering questions. I was asked not to inquire about their families and home situation. I asked three girls who they wanted to be when they grow up and was told that all want to be teachers. They behaved as children would during recess, playing and running around, while they did so with dignity – without shrieking. The most popular schoolyard game was gati that entails throwing six little rocks or balls in the air and trying to catch them. Allah willing The teachers at Fatima Zahra are theoretically paid 8,000 afghanis a month (€66), up from 6,000 afghanis (€50) last year. However, the afghani has lost much of its value since the Taliban took over, with 6,000 afghanis a year ago worth as much as 8,000 today. However, all of it is merely theoretical for the teachers who are not paid anything as things stand. “It is alright,” Hajeera Sadaqat said when asked about missed salary. “We will make do. Inshallah!” – God willing. A girls’ school in Jalalabad. Photo: Erik Prozes NGO Mondo that pursues humanitarian projects in Africa and Asia has spent around €150,000 on the Fatima Zahra school over the last decade. “We have paid the salaries of the teachers and bought school aids for the children every year. A few years ago, we helped the school install solar panels and get power,” said Riina Kuusik-Rajasaar, head of Afghanistan projects at Mondo. “The school has also gotten an annex – two classrooms for science classes for older students.” Jamila Hakim said that the school would not exist without Estonia. “We are all immensely grateful to Estonia and the Estonian people for their help,” the principal said. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwp9.text: Image source, BBC News Ukraine Image caption, Daria left her apartment in Kyiv this summer after Russia's attacks on the city intensified By Diana Kuryshko and Victoria Kalimbet BBC News Ukrainian Published 3 hours ago For much of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Daria was not afraid of the shelling. Even on nights of heavy bombardment, the 27-year-old could sleep through the explosions in her apartment in Kyiv. Like many Ukrainians, she relied on the "two-wall rule": staying safe by keeping two walls between herself and the outside world. But this year that has changed. In recent months, Russia has scaled up the intensity and frequency of its attacks against the Ukrainian capital. In the first 10 days of July alone, the Russians launched dozens of ballistic missiles in three major attacks, killing nearly 60 civilians, according to official figures. Similar large scale attacks took place in August and September. A BBC Verify analysis of government figures found Kyiv is now suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. It was during an attack one night in May that Daria realised she no longer felt safe in her home. She and her boyfriend were in the corridor of their ninth-floor apartment, watching a boxing match, as explosions went off around them, the blast waves causing the windows to repeatedly slam open and shut. When the fight ended, "there was no longer anything to distract me," Daria says. "That's when I realised I was really scared." At first, she thought she would start using a nearby bomb shelter during attacks. But in June, when a young mother was killed running to a shelter in Kyiv, Daria decided she needed to leave the city altogether. She returned to her family's country house, 30km (18.6 miles) away in Romankiv, and now spends a total of four hours a day commuting to and from Kyiv, where she works in the defence sector. Image source, Ukraine State Emergency Service Image caption, A photo from the State Emergency Service shows the impact of a Russian strike in July Daria's experience is far from unique. Residents in Kyiv who say they had got used to Russia's missile and drone strikes have told the BBC World Service the renewed intensity of the attacks is making them rethink how they live their lives. Previously, Ukraine's air-defence network and military intelligence gave residents a degree of predictability. Large-scale attacks could often be detected in advance, allowing people to spend the night in shelters, leave the city or take other precautions. But since the summer, Russia has changed its tactics. It has relied less on aircraft, whose movements can be spotted ahead of time, and more on ballistic missiles that travel at tremendous speed and provide little warning. Air-raid alerts sometimes begin only moments before impact, or even simultaneously with the first explosions. Daria can see her nearest shelter from the window of her apartment, which she still rents. Even so, it takes around 10 minutes to reach it. During a ballistic attack, she might have just four minutes' warning or less, she says. She decided to leave Kyiv in June after holidaying abroad this summer and seeing people living "normal" lives. Since then, she has only spent one night in Kyiv. Image caption, Ballistic missiles are difficult to detect in advance Yet, for many, leaving is not an option. Sixty-two-year-old Olha Vlasova lives on the seventh floor of a high-rise apartment block with her 98-year-old mother, Nadia Tsybina. Despite her age, Nadia remains intensely engaged with the world. From her bed she follows events in Ukraine and abroad, discussing everything from US President Donald Trump's policies, to anti-corruption protests in Kyiv, and the Epstein files. She's also learned that she can often tell, simply by listening, whether a Russian missile or drone has been intercepted or has reached its target. This summer, she says she has heard fewer interceptions. "It's upsetting when there's nothing to shoot them down with," Nadia says. "I can hear them firing with whatever they've got, rifles, machine guns." Image source, BBC News Ukraine Image caption, Nadia, 98, continues to follow world events closely from her bed Image source, BBC News Ukraine Image caption, Olha has taken to placing a mattress by the window to protect her and her mother from flying glass With Nadia confined to her bed, she and Olha cannot go to a shelter, however serious an attack is. Instead, as soon as an air-raid siren sounds, Olha covers her mother with a blanket, pushes a mattress into their window frame, and then hides in a wardrobe which puts two walls between her and outside. Nadia places a pillow over her head to protect her face from flying glass. Once in her wardrobe, Olha will often stay awake watching the news all night. "They come in, they bomb us," Nadia says. "You haven't even had time to fall asleep, and there's another alert. They come again, they shoot them down again. And it goes on all night. "People don't sleep, and then they walk around like zombies." Image source, Global Images Ukraine via Getty Images Image caption, The new academic year in Kyiv began with many students attending classes in shelters as an air raid alert was in effect in the morning An increase in daytime attacks means life in Kyiv is now interrupted by air raid sirens day and night. At the beginning of September, when children returned to school after the summer break, there were dozens of air raid alerts, followed by explosions and fires. According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, two children were injured in attacks on 31 August. As a result, many children stayed at home, while others spent hours in the basements of schools and kindergartens. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Commuters in Kyiv have become accustomed to long wait times as the metro is disrupted. When the sirens sound, it also affects businesses and transport. Shopping centres close and above-ground metro stations suspend operations, often severing public transport links between Kyiv's Left and Right Banks, on either side of the Dnieper River, for hours at a time. New metro operating rules during air raid alerts are being introduced in an attempt to improve the situation. For Olha, it has meant seeing less of her eight-year-old granddaughter, who lives on the other side of the city. She knows if her granddaughter comes to visit, she risks struggling to return home. When metro services stop running, expensive cab journeys are Olha's only option. Crossing the river can cost as much as 1,000 hryvnias ($22, Â£16.6), she says, just under one-eighth of Ukraine's monthly minimum wage. The experience has left her frustrated with what she sees as hesitation by some of Ukraine's foreign partners to provide additional air-defence missiles. President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly appealed to allies for additional air-defence systems and interceptor missiles. "They [Ukraine's allies] wait, thinking: 'What if we get attacked?'" Olha says. "It's like refusing to give medicine to a cancer patient because you're saying, 'What if I get sick one day?' Well, maybe you won't. Give it away before it expires." Image source, Natalia Bushkovska Image caption, Neither Natalia nor her daughter can sleep through the nightly attacks In another part of the city, mother-of-two Natalia Bushkovska each night rehearses three different plans. Plan A is to spread bedding in the hallway behind two interior walls; Plan B is to move the family into the building's shared corridor; and Plan C is to head for the basement. Even there, she admits, she does not feel entirely safe. "I keep a backpack with essential items," says Natalia, 37. "There's a tourniquet for severe bleeding. I also keep a whistle, just in case. "If the worst happens, rescuers will be able to find us under the rubble." Her nine-year-old daughter has her own emergency bag containing toys, lip balm and a tourniquet. Like her 12-year-old brother, she learned how to use a tourniquet through first-aid training. Natalia says the constant attacks are exhausting. While her son often sleeps through them, she and her daughter wake up almost every time. "Because of the attacks, I don't get enough sleep," she says. "Now, in the fifth year of the war, I find it increasingly difficult to bounce back after nights like these." The growing intensity of the strikes, she says, is taking a psychological toll across the city. "People are exhausted. They don't have enough time to recover." On Thursday 17 September, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. According to Mayor Vitali Klitschko, 20 people were injured in the attack. Among the wounded were two children, aged 10 and 12. http://www.theuknews.com/news/279313387/.text: Adviser denies same-sex union abroad offers a ticket to stay in EU CN 17 Sep 2026, 17:03 GMT+10 (CN) - A trip to Italy made their union legal but shouldn't give a same-sex couple the right to live together in Romania, an adviser to the EU's top court said Thursday. Advocate General Laila Medina advised the Court of Justice of the European Union that EU law did not require Romania to grant residence to FV, a British woman who entered a civil union with her Romanian partner in Italy. FV is challenging an order to leave Romania so the two women can continue living together. The women lived continents apart when they formalized their relationship in June 2024, with FV in Australia and her partner, GH, in Romania. FV joined GH the following January in Romania, where GH cared for her severely disabled mother. Neither had lived in Italy. Medina wrote: "Although entering into a civil union is a legal act of undoubted personal significance, it is not equivalent to having lived as a family in the host member state." Her nonbinding opinion explained why EU law protected family life developed during genuine residence abroad: Citizens might otherwise hesitate to move if they could not bring their families home afterward. Extending those protections to a brief visit, she warned, would intrude on national authority over family law and decisions reserved for EU lawmakers. Medina also found no evidence that GH depended on FV so completely that denying FV residence would force GH to leave Romania or the EU, though the national court would have to verify that assessment. Without the necessary connection to EU law, the bloc's fundamental rights charter did not apply. European human rights protections remained relevant. FV had applied to extend her stay in February 2025. Immigration officials ordered her to return to Britain in April because the couple have no children together and FV had not demonstrated residence rights elsewhere in the EU as a Romanian citizen's family member. Lenka Kikova, an assistant professor of law at Masaryk University, said the judges had an opportunity to clarify how much more than a border crossing EU residence protections required. "In particular, the question is whether it is enough for the EU citizen to travel to another member state for the sole purpose of entering into a civil union there," she said. Kikova said endorsing Medina's approach could also reassure those concerned that citizens could sidestep their own country's family laws simply by formalizing a relationship abroad. Alina Tryfonidou, an assistant professor in EU law and family law at the University of Cyprus, saw room for progress on LGBTI rights despite the proposed outcome. "The advocate general makes clear that failure to qualify as a family member under EU residence rules does not end the inquiry," she said. If EU law applied, she explained, authorities would still have to assess the couple's relationship individually, even if domestic law did not recognize their union. Tryfonidou also highlighted the unequal choices Romania's rules left couples: Opposite-sex partners could marry to qualify for family reunification, while same-sex partners could not. She said that disadvantage was tied specifically to sexual orientation. Although it did not change Medina's proposed outcome, she said the equality argument could prove important in a future case covered by EU law. Medina also explained how FV's application would have to be handled if the court rejected her conclusion that EU law did not apply. Romania would have to consider the couple's relationship individually, rather than dismiss it because their union was not recognized. The requirements officials had relied on, a shared child or prior registration as a family member elsewhere in the EU, went beyond the relevant EU rules, she said. That would give FV a right to an individual assessment and reasons for any refusal, but would not guarantee permission to stay. FV's lawyers were not been publicly identified at the opinion stage. Romania's General Inspectorate for Immigration did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The final word on FV's right to stay is still to come. Medina's opinion is nonbinding, and the EU court must now give its ruling before the Court of Appeal in Oradea decides her challenge, with no ordinary appeal available. Courthouse News reporter Eunseo Hong is based in the Netherlands . https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/10/20/vite.text: Menü Kereső Ugyanaz a cég újíthatja fel az Iparművészeti Múzeumot, mint az Igazságügyi Palotát Belföld Nádor András Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Teljesen átszervezhetik az állami beruházásokkal foglalkozó cégeket, az Igazságügyi Palota rekonstrukcióját végző Steindl Imre Program Nonprofit Zrt. (SIP) állíthatja helyre az Iparművészeti Múzeumot – ilyen bejelentéseket tett Vitézy Dávid közlekedési és beruházási miniszter egy keddi sajtótájékoztatón, amit a felújított Igazságügyi Palota bejárásán tartott. A Válasz Online beszámolója szerint az Igazságügyi Palota előzetes regisztráció után négy napig ingyenesen látogatható lesz. Mivel a kormány elégedett azzal, ahogy a tavaly meghalt Wachsler Tamás által létrehozott állami cég, a Steindl Imre Program Nonprofit Zrt. (SIP) az Igazságügyi Palota és a szomszédos Agrárminisztérium rekonstrukcióját megrendelői oldalról lebonyolította, ezért továbbra is számít a cégben dolgozókra az állami műemléki projekteknél. Ilyen projekt például az Iparművészeti Múzeum felújítása, amit szintén a SIP kapott meg. Az Igazságügyi Palota melletti épület, ami korábban az Agrárminisztériumnak adott otthont, még messze van a befejezéstől, várhatóan 2028-ra készülhet majd el. Az Orbán-kormány úgy akarta ezt átterveztetni, hogy akár négy évre, egy teljes ciklusra is alkalmas legyen az Országgyűlés elhelyezésére, mert úgy volt, a Parlamentet felújítják. Vitézy szerint az Agrárminisztérium átterveztetése miatt hónapokra megakadt a munka, az új kormány úgy döntött, visszavonja az előző kormány döntését, mert nincs szükség az Országgyűlés kiköltöztetésére. Az újságírók megkérdezték a minisztert, valóban beköltözhet-e az Agrárminisztérium épületébe majd a Miniszterelnökség. Vitézy erre sejtelmes választ adott: azt mondta, a felújított épület alkalmas lesz bármely nagy, 6-700 fős minisztérium elhelyezésére. A miniszter bejelentette: létrejön a Hild Központ, ami a beruházási tárca alá tartozó cégeket fogja tömöríteni egy központi holdingba. Ez alá fog tartozni a SIP Zrt., a Hungexpo beruházásaival foglalkozó Expo Park Kft. és egy olyan cég, ami a Millenáris és a budai Vár közterület-üzemeltetési és kulturális programszervezői feladataival foglalkozik. A Hild Központ leginkább várostervezési és városfejlesztési feladatokkal foglalkozik majd, ezért menedzselni fogja Rákosrendező és a ferencvárosi Diákváros projektjeit is. Vitézy kedden bejelentette: a főváros és az állam egy közös fejlesztőcég létrehozásáról állapodott meg, ennek az állami része a Hild Központnál lesz. Șefa diplomației europene, Kaja Kallas, a declarat că și-a dorit să fie desemnată emisar special al Uniunii Europene pentru negocierile de pace legate de încetarea războiului din Ucraina, potrivit Euronews preluat de MEDIAFAX . Aceasta a precizat că acest rol îi revine în mod firesc, având în vedere funcția pe care o ocupă, însă a adăugat că Rusia nu o dorește la masa negocierilor din cauza pozițiilor sale ferme. „Rușii nu mă vor”, a spus Kaja Kallas vineri dimineață, înaintea summitului informal al liderilor UE de la Dublin, în Irlanda. „Dar avem noi vreun cuvânt de spus în privința a cine reprezintă Rusia? Nu, nu avem. În realitate, trebuie să avem o echipă puternică”, a declarat aceasta. Potrivit acesteia, liderii europeni au numit-o Înalt Reprezentant în iunie 2024, știind că, în timpul mandatului său de cinci ani, vor fi necesare negocieri în mod direct cu Moscova. „În iunie 2024, liderii au luat o decizie cu privire la cine va reprezenta [UE] în chestiunile de securitate și politică externă. Și s-a discutat faptul că, în acești cinci ani, vor avea loc negocieri cu rușii”, a spus Kaja Kallas. Ea a mai spus că liderii pot schimba această decizie, dacă își doresc acest lucru, dar discuțiile ar trebui să se concentreze în mod special pe problemele care sunt prioritar de rezolvat. „Dacă liderii doresc să modifice acea înțelegere, o pot face, desigur, întrucât este decizia lor, dar cred că ar trebui să ne concentrăm energia, de fapt, pe fondul problemelor”, a afirmat șefa diplomației europene. Ea a mai spus că UE nu ar trebui să urmeze modelul Statelor Unite, care au desemnat doi reprezentanți aleși personal, Steve Witkoff și Jared Kushner, pentru discuțiile de pace. Potrivit spuselor sale, Europa ar trebui să aleagă o persoană care are deja un rol instituțional. Tratatul de la Lisabona îi încredințează Înaltului Reprezentant coordonarea și punerea în aplicare a politicii externe a UE. De asemenea, președintele Consiliului European, funcție ocupată în prezent de Antonio Costa, are un rol de reprezentare. Comisia Europeană se ocupă, la rândul său, de domenii importante pentru negocieri, precum sancțiunile, finanțarea și procesul de aderare. Antonio Costa a devenit destul de repede principalul favorit pentru funcția de emisar special, în timp ce Kaja Kallas este considerată la Bruxelles o figură controversată, care a fost tot mai mult lăsată în afara discuțiilor la nivel înalt. Întrebată despre această situație, Kallas a spus că trebuie să respecte pozițiile statelor membre, în condițiile în care politica externă a UE se bazează pe principiul unanimității. „Sunt ținută de ceea ce spun statele membre. Nu mă reprezint pe mine însămi. Reprezint 27 de state, așa cum o fac deja de doi ani”, a declarat ea. Întrebată dacă opoziția Rusiei față de numirea sa are legătură și cu faptul că provine din Europa de Est, Kallas a spus că Moscova nu și-ar dori la negocieri nicio persoană care să aibă o poziție puternică. „Vor să-și impună pretențiile maxime, așa cum au făcut întotdeauna”, a spus ea, respingând „amenințările și ultimatumurile”. „Desigur, atunci când negociezi cu cineva, îți dorești ca cealaltă parte să fie cât mai slabă posibil, pentru a obține ceea ce vrei. Este foarte clar”, a continuat ea. Totuși, șefa diplomației europene a mai adăugat că Moscova nu trebuie să aibă dreptul de a decide cine reprezintă Uniunea Europeană. „Dar nu depinde de ei să decidă acest lucru. Altfel, dacă le oferim acest drept, le oferim, de fapt, un avantaj pe care nu ar trebui să-l aibă”, a adăugat Kallas. Rusii + Trump vor doar pupincurisri. Nu vor negociere, vor diktat.
